summary: Companion to the document on GMPLS support for Metro Ethernet Forum and G.8011 Ethernet service switching, applied to the user network interface. It describes how a customer-side device can request those Ethernet services from a provider network using GMPLS.

eli5.summary: This is the customer-door version of the rules. It shows how a customer asks the carrier for an Ethernet connection using GMPLS messages.

questions: how does a customer request ethernet service with gmpls
what are epl and evpl ethernet services
what is the unknown endpoint error in rsvp
how does a uni client find the egress ip address
subtitle: How a customer's edge node asks a provider network for an Ethernet connection using GMPLS signaling.

tldr.problem: Ethernet services defined by the Metro Ethernet Forum and ITU G.8011 need a way for a customer's edge node to request connections from a provider network by signaling, but the edge node may not know the far end's IP address.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reuses the GMPLS overlay UNI procedures and the Ethernet extensions of RFC 6004, and adds a Notify-based address resolution step plus a rule for changing the VLAN ID at the egress of an EVPL service.
tldr.outcome: It adds very little on top of existing GMPLS signaling: one resolution procedure, one VLAN ID rule and one new RSVP error value, Unknown Endpoint.

today: RFC 6005 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2010, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is meant to be read together with RFC 6004.

sections.title: Scope and Reference Model
sections.content:
The Metro Ethernet Forum (MEF) and ITU-T G.8011 define Ethernet services for transport networks, including the Ethernet Private Line (EPL) and Ethernet Virtual Private Line (EVPL) services. RFC 6005 describes how GMPLS can control Label Switched Paths (LSPs) that carry those services at the User Network Interface (UNI).

The reference model has edge nodes (EN) that connect to Ethernet networks and core nodes (CN) in the provider network. The UNI function in an edge node is the UNI-C (client) and the one in a core node is the UNI-N (network). What happens inside the core network is out of scope: the RFC does not define or limit the technology used there.

It builds on RFC 4208 (the GMPLS overlay model), RFC 6004 (Ethernet service switching) and RFC 6002. It is the UNI companion to RFC 6004.
sections.eli5: A customer's building plugs into the phone company's network at a front door called the UNI. This RFC only covers what happens at that front door, not inside the phone company.

sections.title: Which Services and Control Modes Are Covered
sections.content:
The RFC supports point-to-point (P2P) service. Multipoint-to-multipoint (MP2MP) service is required by G.8011 and MEF 11, but, as in RFC 6004, it is left for future study and not addressed here.

MEF 11 defines three types of UNI control. In Type 1 services are configured manually. In Type 2 they may be configured manually or through a link management interface. In Type 3 they can be established and managed through a signaling interface. This document targets Type 3 only.

Apart from the changes described in the RFC, existing procedures for RSVP objects are not modified, and those in RFC 6002, RFC 6004, RFC 4208 and RFC 4974 MUST be followed.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to order a connection: by hand, by hand with a helper tool, or by sending messages automatically. This RFC is only about the automatic way.

sections.title: UNI Addressing and Endpoint Identification
sections.content:
LSPs controlled under this RFC MUST use the addressing and procedures of RFC 4208. This includes putting the egress edge node's IP address in the endpoint address field of the SESSION object.

The catch is that the ingress edge node may not have that address. The request that starts a connection might only name the far Ethernet endpoint. Ethernet endpoint (UNI) identification otherwise follows RFC 6004, with one extra case covered by the address resolution procedure.
sections.eli5: To mail a letter you need the street address. Sometimes the customer only knows the name of the person to reach, so the address has to be looked up first.

sections.title: Address Resolution with Notify
sections.content:
When an edge node has the egress Ethernet endpoint identifier but not its IP address, it MUST send a Notify message as described in RFC 4974. The message MUST carry a CALL_ATTRIBUTES object with the Endpoint ID TLV from RFC 6004, and the tunnel endpoint address of the SESSION object MUST be set to zero (0). It is sent to an address of the first core node.

A core node (UNI-N) that receives such a Notify MUST find the Endpoint ID TLV. If the object or TLV is missing, it MUST discard the message and MUST NOT send a Message ID Acknowledgment. Otherwise it MUST map the endpoint ID to an IP address of the egress edge node and set the endpoint address field of the SESSION object to it, then continue standard RFC 4974 processing.

If no address can be found, the node MUST send an error Notify (Section 6.2.2 of RFC 4974). The error code and value SHOULD be Routing Problem/Unknown Endpoint (error code 24, error value 35).

When the ingress receives the response Notify, it SHOULD identify the call from the Endpoint ID TLV and, if they were not zero in the setup Notify, the short and long Call IDs. The returned address MUST be used in all later messages for that Ethernet connection.
sections.eli5: The customer asks the carrier, "Who is Bob's mailbox?" The carrier looks it up and answers with the address. If the carrier cannot find Bob, it sends back an error that says so.

sections.title: Connection Identification and Call IDs
sections.content:
UNI signaling for Ethernet connections MUST follow the connection identification procedures of RFC 6004, with one exception. The procedures of Section 7.2 of RFC 4974 MAY be used so that the first core node, rather than the initiating edge node, allocates the Call IDs.

The address resolution procedure above MAY be used whether the Call IDs are generated by the initiating UNI or by the first core node.
sections.eli5: Each connection needs a ticket number. Usually the customer picks it, but this RFC lets the carrier hand out the number instead.

sections.title: EPL and EVPL Services
sections.content:
For EPL, there are no additional UNI-specific requirements. The procedures of RFC 6004, as modified by the sections above, MUST be followed.

For EVPL there is one extra requirement. MEF 6 allows the single VLAN ID used at the ingress UNI to be mapped to a different VLAN ID at the egress UNI, for EVPL services that do not support both bundling and VLAN ID preservation. Such a mapping MUST be requested and signaled with the explicit label control mechanism of RFC 4208, and not the mechanisms of RFC 6004. When explicit label control is not used, VLAN IDs MUST be preserved, meaning they are not modified across the LSP.
sections.eli5: A private line needs no special extras. A virtual line may relabel the customer's traffic tag at the far end, but only if the customer asks for that in a specific way. Otherwise the tag stays the same.

sections.title: IANA Assignment
sections.content: IANA assigned error value 35, Unknown Endpoint, under error code 24 (Routing Problem) in the "Error Codes and Globally-Defined Error Value Sub-Codes" part of the RSVP Parameters registry. Error code 24 itself comes from RFC 3209.
sections.eli5: The official list of error messages got one new line: "Unknown Endpoint".

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC uses the mechanisms of RFC 6004 and RFC 4974 and does not itself change the security models of either. It notes that the address resolution step parallels the replacement of information that occurs under Section 7.2 of RFC 4974. Readers are pointed to those two RFCs for the relevant security considerations.
sections.eli5: This RFC adds no new locks or keys. It relies on the ones from the RFCs it builds on.
